newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: Australia's North buys stake in Canadian iron ore miner.
newsitem.headline: Australia's North buys stake in Canadian iron ore miner.

text.p: Australian miner North Ltd said Friday it bought a majority stake in Canada's biggest iron ore producer, paying a total of $230 million to Bethlehem Steel Corp. and National Steel Corp. of the United States.
North said the deal gives it a 59.3 percent stake in the Iron Ore Co. of Canada.

Bethlehem Steel said it agreed to sell its 37.57 percent equity interest in IOCC to North in a transaction that will result in cash proceeds of about $145 million. It said it will continue to purchase iron ore from Iron Ore of Canada under a long-term contract.
As part of the deal, National Steel Corp. also agreed to sell its 21.73 percent equity interest in the Canadian company.
"This purchase ... positions North as a major player in the world's iron ore industry," North managing director Campbell Anderson told a news conference.
North already reaps 14.7 million metric tons of iron ore each year from its majority-owned Robe River mine in northwest Australia. Its IOCC stake adds about nine million tons a year.
IOCC, with its higher quality iron ore and presence in U.S. and European markets, will expand North's global reach, which has so far been confined to steel-hungry Asia, Anderson said.
"As an established producer, IOCC will have immediate positive impact on North's earnings ...," he said.
Iron Ore has iron ore production facilities in Labrador City, Newfoundland and ore shipping facilities in Sept-Iles, Quebec. It produces about 15 million tons of iron ore annually.
North's announcement follows two recent acquisitions in copper and zinc and is part of a strategy to firm up sagging profits and become a global player in metal commodities.
Weak metals prices and a strong Australian dollar have sent earnings into a slide in recent years, intensifying North's search for new growth opportunities.
North Friday posted a 55 percent rise in profits for the six months to Dec. 31, largely due to improved performances in its iron ore, copper and uranium operations.

It said the second half of 1996/97 would be even stronger and the outlook for 1997/98 brighter still, with the start-up in August of the huge Alumbrera copper-gold mine in Argentina. North owns 25 percent of the project.
But some industry analysts sounded a warning about North's latest foray, citing IOCC's high production costs and the uncertain outlook for iron ore.
"There's a risk of the iron ore price coming down in real terms in the next two to three years," one analyst told Reuters.
North conceded IOCC's production costs per ton were relatively high, but said it was confident it could slash costs and foreshadowed major staff cuts.
"Changes in the work force are subject to discussions with the unions, but we do see a considerable reduction," Anderson said, adding he did not anticipate union unrest.
But Bell Securities analyst Rob Craigie said he remained to be convinced that the costs could be pared back sufficently.
"Clearly they have ideas on how to reduce costs but (they are) certainly not convincing. They may be able to, but it's early days," Craigie said.
